planting.note: Sow in fall or cold-stratify seed, since this glade-adapted species germinates best after a period of cold moist chilling; established plants shrug off heat and drought far better than common black-eyed Susan.

directions: This Ozark glade native forms a tidy basal clump before sending up wiry stems topped with orange-yellow rays around a dark, raised cone. Unlike biennial Rudbeckia hirta, it is a true long-lived perennial and tolerates thin, rocky, alkaline soils that would stunt most black-eyed Susans. It draws a wide range of short- and long-tongued bees along with butterflies and beneficial wasps, and rarely needs staking. Deadheading is optional since goldfinches favor the ripened seed heads through winter.

planting.note: Direct sow after frost or set out divisions in spring; adapts to average garden soil and needs little fuss once established.

directions: A regional variety native to Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio, Deam's coneflower carries larger, more coarsely toothed and hairier leaves than the typical species along with slightly smaller flowerheads on taller stems. It spreads gradually by rhizome to form a dependable clump that blooms from midsummer into fall and holds up well without staking. Its late-season nectar and pollen support a broad range of bees and butterflies, and the seed heads feed finches into winter. It is easygoing about soil type as long as drainage is reasonable.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Species Profile

planting.note: Set out nursery plants in spring after frost danger passes; this fine-textured selection needs almost no supplemental water once its roots are established.

directions: Selected from a batch of narrowleaf ironweed seedlings, this vase-shaped cultivar carries thread-fine foliage on stiff upright stems and stays shorter and more floriferous than the wild species. Flat-topped clusters of magenta-purple, fringe-like flowers open in late summer into fall, drawing bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds right up to frost. It thrives in lean to average soil with minimal watering after its first season and rarely needs dividing or staking. Goldfinches and other seed-eating birds visit the dried heads through winter.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center Trial Garden Notes

common_name: Phantom Joe Pye Weed (Compact Hybrid Joe-Pye Weed)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil; this compact hybrid holds its dense habit without the floppy stems that taller Joe-Pye weeds can develop.

directions: A patented hybrid raised from spotted Joe-Pye weed crossed with white snakeroot, 'Phantom' packs the domed, mauve-purple flower clusters of its native parents onto a much shorter, denser plant that needs no staking. Whorled, bold-textured leaves take on a purplish cast in cool weather, and the late-summer blooms are a magnet for swallowtails, bumblebees, and other pollinators. It performs best with steady moisture and appreciates a bit of afternoon shade in hot climates, making it a fit for rain gardens and moist border edges. Deer generally leave it alone.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Comparative Study of Joe-Pye Weeds

common_name: Redshift Coreopsis (Big Bang Series Color-Changing Tickseed)

planting.note: Set out potted plants after frost in well-drained soil; this hybrid is bred from multiple Coreopsis species and does not come true from seed.

directions: Bred by Darrell Probst as part of the Big Bang series, 'Redshift' opens creamy-yellow flowers ringed in red around a golden button center, and the ray color deepens toward solid red as nights cool in fall. Clumping and sturdy-stemmed, it blooms from midsummer through the first hard frost without the sprawl some tickseeds show late in the season. It is highly drought tolerant once rooted in and rarely bothered by pests or disease, making it a low-input choice for pollinator borders. Bees and small butterflies work the flowers steadily through the season.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center Trial Garden Notes

common_name: Honey Bee Blue Korean Mint (Compact Anise Hyssop)

planting.note: Start seed indoors on the soil surface since it needs light to germinate, then transplant out after frost; established plants self-sow lightly and tolerate dry spells well.

directions: This compact selection of Korean mint holds dense spikes of sky-blue flowers above mint-scented foliage on a tidier, more floriferous plant than the straight species. Bees work the blooms constantly from midsummer into early fall, and the aromatic leaves and flowers are edible, giving it a place in both pollinator beds and culinary herb gardens. It tolerates heat and dry soil once established and rarely needs deadheading to keep blooming. Give it full sun and sharp drainage, since wet winter soil is its main limiting factor.

planting.note: Set out plants in spring in evenly moist soil; its dwarf, self-supporting habit means it never needs the pinching or staking taller sneezeweeds often require.

directions: This patented dwarf sneezeweed condenses the daisy-like, chocolate-coned flowers of native Helenium autumnale onto a compact plant well suited to smaller borders and large containers. It begins flowering two to three weeks ahead of typical sneezeweed cultivars and keeps producing gold-and-orange blooms from midsummer into fall. Bees and butterflies visit steadily, and the cut flowers hold up well in water. It prefers consistently moist, fertile soil and full sun, and its neat habit stays upright even in open, windy sites.

common_name: Marshall's Delight Bee Balm (Mildew-Resistant Pink Bergamot)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring with good air circulation and morning sun; water at the soil line rather than overhead to keep this otherwise mildew-resistant selection clean in humid weather.

directions: Bred in Canada for improved disease resistance, this bee balm holds up far better against powdery mildew than older red and scarlet cultivars while still drawing hummingbirds, bumblebees, and clearwing moths to its clear pink, pom-pom flowerheads. It spreads by shallow rhizomes to form a broadening patch and blooms over a long stretch from early to midsummer, especially if spent flower heads are removed. It tolerates a range of soil moisture but colors up best with consistent water and full sun to light shade. Deer and rabbits generally avoid it thanks to the aromatic foliage.
